summary: Defines a data structure that can be appended to selected ICMP messages to identify the interface a datagram arrived on, the interface it would have been forwarded through, and the next hop. This helps with troubleshooting. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router cannot forward a packet it sends an ICMP error back to the sender, but the error usually does not say which interface the packet arrived on or which one it would have gone out of. This document defines an optional extra block for those ICMP messages that names the incoming interface, the outgoing interface or the next hop, using an interface index, an IP address, a name or the MTU.

questions: how to identify next hop in icmp
what is icmp interface information object
how does traceroute identify the incoming interface
what is class-num 2 in icmp extensions
subtitle: A way for routers to say, inside an ICMP error, which interface a packet came in on and where it would have gone next.

tldr.problem: An ICMP error message often does not reveal which interface the failed datagram arrived on, especially for unnumbered interfaces, so traceroute and similar tools cannot name the exact interface.
tldr.mechanism: An Interface Information Object (Class-Num 2) is appended to selected ICMP messages. Its C-Type bits say whether it describes the incoming interface, a sub-IP component, the outgoing interface or the next hop, and which of ifIndex, IP address, name and MTU follow.
tldr.outcome: Operators and tools get explicit interface and next-hop details for troubleshooting. The RFC says the extension is meant for administrative debugging, and implementations should be able to suppress or hide the information.

today: RFC 5837 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the Interface Information Object, an ICMP extension for identifying interfaces and next hops.

sections.title: Why the Source Address Is Not Enough
sections.content:
IP devices use ICMPv4 and ICMPv6 to convey control information. When a device receives a datagram it cannot process, it may send an ICMP message to the datagram's originator, and network operators and higher-level protocols use those messages to detect and diagnose network issues.

In the simplest case the source address of the ICMP message identifies the interface on which the datagram arrived. In many cases, though, the incoming interface is not identified by the ICMP message at all. According to RFC 1812, when a router generates an ICMPv4 message, the source address of that message MUST be one of the IP addresses associated with the physical interface over which the message is transmitted, or, if that interface has no IP addresses associated with it, the device's router ID or host ID is used instead.

The source address of the ICMPv4 message identifies the interface on which the original datagram arrived only if all of the following hold: the device sends the message through the same interface on which the datagram was received, and that interface is numbered. The incoming and outgoing interfaces may differ because of an asymmetric return path, which can come from asymmetric link costs, parallel links or equal cost multipath. RFC 1122 gives similar guidance for source address selection on multihomed IPv4 hosts, and those recommendations do not always make the source address identify the incoming interface either.

ICMPv6 is somewhat more flexible: for responses to messages sent to a non-local interface, the source address must be a unicast address belonging to the node, and it SHOULD be chosen by the rules used for any other packet the node originates, given the destination address, although it MAY be selected in an alternative way if that would lead to a more informative choice of address reachable from the destination.

When a datagram that cannot be processed arrives on an unnumbered interface, neither ICMPv4 nor ICMPv6 is currently able to identify the incoming interface. Even when an ICMP message is generated so that its source address identifies the incoming interface, the receiver of that message has no way of knowing that this is the case. ICMP extensions are therefore required to identify the incoming interface explicitly.

With this extension, a device can explicitly identify the incoming IP interface or its sub-IP components by any combination of ifIndex, IPv4 address, IPv6 address, name and MTU. The interface name SHOULD be identical to the first 63 octets of the ifName as defined in the Interfaces Group MIB, and the ifIndex is defined there too. The same extension can identify the outgoing interface over which the datagram would have been forwarded if it had been forwardable, and the IP next hop to which it would have been forwarded. The next-hop information can be used for creating a downstream map, but it may not always be available: there are corner cases where it does not exist, and there may be implementations where it is not practical to provide it. The specification therefore provides an encoding for the next-hop IP address when it is available.

The extension uses the ICMP multi-part message framework of RFC 4884, and the same backward compatibility issues that apply to that framework apply here.
sections.plainLanguage: The address in the error message comes from the outgoing interface, not the incoming one, and an interface with no address of its own cannot be named that way at all. So the router has to say it explicitly, and this document defines how that is encoded.

sections.title: What the Extra Information Is Good For
sections.content:
The extensions give traceroute more to work with. An enhanced traceroute application, like older implementations, identifies the nodes a datagram visited on its way to its destination, and it differs in that it can explicitly identify at each node the IP interface on which the datagram arrived, the sub-IP component of that interface, the IP interface through which the datagram would have been forwarded had it been forwardable, and the IP next hop to which it would have been forwarded. It can identify those entities by ifIndex, IPv4 address, IPv6 address, name and MTU.

The ifIndex can be used within a management domain to map to an actual interface, and it is also valuable in public applications, where it serves as an opaque token to discern whether two ICMP messages generated by the same router involve the same interface.

A more general application is to identify which outgoing interface triggered a given function for the original packet. If an access control list drops the packet and the router answers with Destination Unreachable or Admin Prohibited, knowing the outgoing interface can be useful. Another example is supporting Path MTU Discovery, because that would allow identification of which outgoing interface cannot support a given MTU size, so that an informed request could be made to reconfigure the MTU of that interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Traceroute is the main use: at each hop it can now say which interface the probe came in on and which one it would have left by. The same block helps with access control lists and with finding the link that cannot carry a large enough packet.

sections.title: The Interface Information Object
sections.content:
The Interface Information Object is an ICMP extension object with a Class-Num of 2, and it can be appended to the ICMPv4 Time Exceeded, ICMPv4 Destination Unreachable and ICMPv4 Parameter Problem messages, and to the ICMPv6 Time Exceeded and ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable messages. For the reasons given in RFC 4884, it cannot be appended to any other currently defined ICMPv4 or ICMPv6 message. It MAY be appended to any of the listed messages, and SHOULD be appended whenever it is required to identify an unnumbered interface and when local policy or security considerations do not supersede that requirement.

A single ICMP message can contain as few as zero and as many as four instances of the object. More than four is illegal, because that would mean an interface role was used more than once. One instance describes one interface role: the IP interface on which a datagram arrived, the sub-IP component of an IP interface on which a datagram arrived, the IP interface through which the datagram would have been forwarded had it been forwardable, or the IP next hop to which the datagram would have been forwarded. Examples of sub-IP components are an Ethernet link aggregation group member, a multilink PPP bundle member and a multilink frame relay bundle member.

To keep the number of octets small, four pieces of information can appear in the object. The ifIndex of the interface may be included, the 32-bit value assigned by the device as specified by the Interfaces Group MIB. An IP Address Sub-Object may be included if the eliciting datagram is IPv4 and the identified interface has at least one IPv4 address, or if the datagram is IPv6 and the interface has at least one IPv6 address. An Interface Name Sub-Object of no more than 63 octets may be included, which SHOULD be the MIB-II ifName but MAY be some other human-meaningful name. A 32-bit unsigned integer reflecting the MTU may be included.

The C-Type indicates both the role of the interface and which information is included. Bits 0 and 1 hold the interface role: value 0 for the IP interface on which a datagram arrived, value 1 for the sub-IP component of that interface, value 2 for the IP interface through which the datagram would have been forwarded, and value 3 for the IP next hop to which it would have been forwarded. Bits 2 and 3 are reserved for future use and MUST be set to zero and ignored on receipt. Bit 4 says that the 32-bit ifIndex is included, bit 5 that an IP Address Sub-Object is present, bit 6 that an Interface Name Sub-Object is included, and bit 7 that the 32-bit MTU is present.

The information included does not identify itself, so the specification fixes the order in which it is sent: if bit 4 is set the ifIndex MUST be sent first, then the IP Address Sub-Object if bit 5 is set, then the Interface Name Sub-Object if bit 6 is set, then the MTU if bit 7 is set. Any or all of the pieces may be present or absent as the C-Type indicates, and any data that follows these optional pieces MUST be ignored. Receiving an object with bits 4, 5, 6 and 7 all zero is valid, though pointless until more bits are assigned, and it MUST NOT generate a warning or an error.
sections.plainLanguage: The object has two jobs: say which interface it is talking about, and carry the details of that interface. Two bits give the role, four more say whether the index, the address, the name and the MTU are present, and the details always appear in that order so a reader knows what is what.

sections.title: The Address and Name Sub-Objects
sections.content:
The Interface IP Address Sub-Object begins with a 16-bit Address Family Identifier, which identifies the type of address in the IP Address field and determines the length of that field and of the whole sub-object. The valid values are a subset of the IANA registry of Address Family Numbers: 1 for a 32-bit IPv4 address and 2 for a 128-bit IPv6 address. The next 16 bits are reserved, MUST be set to zero and ignored on receipt. The IP Address field itself is variable length and holds an address associated with the identified interface. If the eliciting datagram was IPv4, the sub-object MUST represent an IPv4 address, and if it was IPv6, an IPv6 address.

The Interface Name Sub-Object begins with a length byte followed by the interface name octets. The length of the sub-object MUST be a multiple of 4 octets and MUST NOT exceed 64 octets, and the length field covers the length byte and the name. The limit is there to leave room for the start of the original packet and for additional information. The name SHOULD be the full MIB-II ifName if that is less than 64 octets, or the first 63 octets of the ifName if it is longer, and it MAY be some other human-meaningful name of the interface. It is useful to provide the ifName for cross-correlation with other MIB information and for human familiarity. The name MUST be padded with ASCII NULL characters if the object would not otherwise terminate on a 4-octet boundary, and it MUST be represented in the UTF-8 charset using the default language.
sections.plainLanguage: The address sub-object starts with a two-byte field saying whether the address is IPv4 or IPv6, then the address itself. The name sub-object starts with its length and then the name, padded so that the whole thing lands on a four-byte boundary, with a hard limit of 64 octets so that room is left for the rest of the ICMP message.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The document shows a full ICMPv4 Time Exceeded message including an Interface Information Object, which must be preceded by an ICMP Extension Structure Header and an ICMP Object Header, both defined in RFC 4884. The example uses an Interface Name Sub-Object of length 64, which is only for illustration and shows the maximum allowable length.

Four further examples show the object on its own. One represents an incoming interface identified by ifIndex and Name, with C-Type 00001010b and Length 72, being 4 for the object header, 4 for the ifIndex and 64 for the name. A second represents an incoming interface identified by ifIndex, IPv4 address and Name, with C-Type 00001110b and Length 80. A third represents an incoming interface identified by ifIndex and IPv6 address, with C-Type 00001100b and Length 28. The last represents an outgoing interface identified by ifIndex and Name, with C-Type 10001010b and Length 72.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the same block with different pieces of information in it: an interface named by its index and name, one that also carries an IPv4 address, one that carries an IPv6 address instead, and one that describes the outgoing interface rather than the incoming one. The length in each case is the sum of the parts.

sections.title: Rules for Using the Object
sections.content:
Multiple Interface Information Objects MAY be included in a single ICMP message, provided that each specifies a unique role, and a single message MUST NOT contain two objects that specify the same role.

The ifIndex, MTU and name information MAY be included whenever it is available, and more than one instance of each of those three information elements MUST NOT be included per object. A single instance of IP address information MAY be included under two circumstances: the eliciting datagram is IPv4 and an IPv4 address is associated with the identified interface, in which case an included IP Address Sub-Object must specify an IPv4 address; or the eliciting datagram is IPv6 and an IPv6 address is associated with the identified interface, in which case it must specify an IPv6 address. In all other circumstances IP address information MUST NOT be included.

An ICMP message that does not conform to these rules and contains multiple instances of the same information is considered illegal, specifically a message containing more than one Interface Information Object with the same role, and a message containing a duplicate information element in a given role. If such an illegal ICMP message is received, it MUST be silently discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Each role may appear only once in a message, and each kind of detail only once per object. An address is only allowed when the datagram that caused the error and the interface address are of the same family. A message that breaks these rules is dropped without a complaint.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension can give the user of traceroute additional network information that is not currently available. Implementations SHOULD provide configuration switches that suppress the generation of the extension based on role, that is the incoming interface, the outgoing interface or the sub-IP data, and SHOULD also provide configuration switches that conceal various types of information, for example the ifIndex or the interface name.

It may be desirable to provide this information to a particular network's operators and not to others. If such policy controls are wanted, an implementation could determine which sub-objects to include based on the destination IP address of the ICMP message that will contain them, or on the mechanisms described in the traceroute extension work in progress. The IP address could be included for all potential recipients, while the ifIndex and interface name could also be included if the destination IP address is a management address of the network that has administrative control of the router. Another example is providing the detailed information only to ICMP destinations inside the local administrative domain, and only traditional information to external or untrusted destinations.

Network address translation needs care as well. Because this extension includes IP addresses, it contains realm-specific information. NAT devices MUST NOT translate or overwrite the extensions described in this document: they must either remove the extension entirely or pass it unchanged. A NAT device might translate an ICMP header without translating the extension, in which case the message could contain two instances of the same address, one translated and one not, so application developers should not assume that addresses in the extension are in the same realm as the addresses in the datagram's header. A NAT device might also translate an ICMPv4 message into ICMPv6 or the reverse, in which case an application could receive an ICMPv6 message with an IPv4 address in the sub-object, or an ICMPv4 message with an IPv6 address in it.

The intended field of use is administrative debugging and troubleshooting, and the mechanisms are not intended for non-debugging applications. This document does not specify an authentication mechanism for the extension it defines, and application developers should be aware that ICMP messages and their contents are easily spoofed.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra detail tells a stranger more about the network than it used to, so a router should be able to switch each role off and to hide the index and the name. NAT devices must pass the block through unchanged or remove it. And because ICMP messages are easy to forge, this is for debugging rather than for applications that depend on the contents.
